title: Painful, stiff hands and wrists in a 35-year-old hairdresser in the rheumatology clinic
desc: This station is a focused history and a rheumatological hand examination of Sarah Little, a 35-year-old hairdresser. Her GP has referred her to the rheumatology outpatient clinic with 3 months of pain and stiffness, worst in her hands and wrists. In Part 2 the candidate interprets her GP's blood results and an X-ray of her right hand and wrist, and diagnoses early seropositive, erosive rheumatoid arthritis. They then plan to start a DMARD safely in a woman who is planning another pregnancy, safety-net and arrange follow-up. They also explain which arthritides classically spare the DIP joints.
focus: Systematic rheumatological hand examination: finding the symmetrical synovitis and DIP sparing of early rheumatoid arthritis, reading an early rheumatoid hand X-ray and starting methotrexate safely in a woman of child-bearing age
stem: You are a medical student in the rheumatology outpatient clinic of a metropolitan hospital. Sarah Little, a 35-year-old woman, has been referred by her GP with pain and stiffness that is worst in her hands and wrists. Her GP organised some tests before the referral. The rheumatology registrar has asked you to see Ms Little first and then report back.
tasks: Take a focused history from Ms Little and perform a focused examination of her hands, telling the examiner what you are examining and describing your findings as you go (10 minutes).

The examiner will give you her blood results and the report of an X-ray of her right hand and wrist. Interpret them, give your most likely diagnosis and differentials, then outline your management and safety netting, and answer the examiner's question (5 minutes).
patient:
Role: You are Sarah Little, a 35-year-old hairdresser. Your date of birth is 29 January 1991. You are sitting in the clinic room and rub your hands from time to time. You are friendly and keen to get answers, but worried. You are right-handed. Give the history below only when asked. When the candidate says what they would examine, the examiner gives the findings from the Exam findings below.

Opening line: "My hands and wrists have been so sore and stiff for months. Some mornings I can barely hold a hairbrush."

The current problem (give only when asked)

  • Joints: the knuckles and the middle joints of your fingers in both hands, and both wrists. Both sides are about the same. The joints at the ends of your fingers are fine. The balls of both feet are sore for the first few steps out of bed.
  • Onset and course: it started about 3 months ago in your right knuckles. Over a few weeks it spread to both hands and both wrists, and it has slowly got worse. It has never gone away completely.
  • Swelling: "My knuckles look puffy, and my wedding ring is too tight now, I can hardly get it off."
  • Character and severity: "A deep ache." 5 out of 10 most of the day, 7 out of 10 first thing in the morning.
  • Morning stiffness: "About an hour and a half before my hands loosen up." It gets better as you use your hands and is worse again after you have been sitting still.
  • Function: you struggle with scissors and blow-drying at work, and you have had to cut back from 4 days a week to 3. Opening jars, doing up your son's buttons and writing are hard.
  • General: "I'm exhausted all the time, even when I sleep well."

Things you do NOT have (say no if asked)

  • No fever, sweats or weight loss.
  • No rash on your face, no rash in the sun, no mouth ulcers and no hair loss. Your fingers do not go white or blue in the cold.
  • No psoriasis or scaly patches on your skin or scalp, and no nail changes. No back pain or back stiffness. No red or painful eyes. No diarrhoea, blood in your stools or bowel problems.
  • No recent illness. If asked about rashes or illness at home: "My son has had the usual childcare colds, but nothing like a rash. I haven't been sick." No overseas travel.
  • No camping, outback travel or mosquito bites in the past few months. You live in the city.
  • No dry eyes or dry mouth. No cough, breathlessness or chest pain.
  • No numbness or pins and needles in your fingers.
  • No injury to your hands. No single joint that has gone suddenly hot and red.

Past medical history

  • Nothing significant. No liver or kidney problems, no stomach ulcers. You have never been told you have hepatitis, and you have never had TB or been in contact with it.
  • One pregnancy (conceived about 5 years ago); normal delivery of your son 4 years ago, with no problems.

Medications and allergies

  • Ibuprofen 400 mg from the chemist, two or three times a day for the last 2 months. "It takes the edge off."
  • The combined oral contraceptive pill.
  • Allergy: Bactrim. Only if asked what happened: "I had it for a bladder infection a few years ago and came out in an itchy rash all over."

Pregnancy plans (only if asked)

  • "We'd like to try for another baby, probably in the next year or so." You are not pregnant; your last period was 2 weeks ago.

Family history

  • Your mother's sister (your aunt) has rheumatoid arthritis. "Her fingers are really bent."
  • Your father has psoriasis on his elbows.
  • Your mother has an underactive thyroid.

Social history

  • You work as a hairdresser in a salon. You live with your husband, Tom, and your 4-year-old son, who goes to childcare.
  • You smoked about 10 cigarettes a day from age 18 and stopped when you became pregnant 5 years ago.
  • Alcohol: a glass or two of wine on a Saturday night.
  • No recreational drugs. You are not of Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander origin.

Ideas, concerns and expectations

  • Ideas: "I wondered if it's from work, all the scissors and blow-drying."
  • Concerns: "My aunt has rheumatoid arthritis and her fingers are all bent. Is that what's going to happen to me?" You are worried about being able to keep working.
  • Expectations: you want to know what it is and to get some treatment that works.

During the examination

  • If the candidate squeezes your knuckles or bends your wrists without warning, wince and pull back. If they ask about pain first and are gentle, you cooperate fully.
  • If asked something not covered here, give a realistic answer that fits the story.

Exam findings (the examiner gives these only when the candidate says what they are examining)

Examiner: read the palpation findings as descriptions. Do not use the word "synovitis"; the candidate must name it.

  • Vital signs (clinic nurse, on arrival): temperature 36.7 °C, HR 76 beats/min regular, BP 116/72 mmHg, RR 14/min, SpO2 99% on room air. Weight 64 kg, height 166 cm.
  • General inspection: well, comfortable at rest, normal build. No Cushingoid features. No walking aids, splints or oxygen.
  • Face, eyes and skin: no malar rash, alopecia or mouth ulcers. Eyes not red; no scleritis or episcleritis. No psoriatic plaques on the scalp, behind the ears, at the umbilicus or in the natal cleft (if asked).
  • Hands, inspection (backs): symmetrical swelling of both wrists, the 2nd and 3rd knuckles of both hands, and the middle joints of the index, middle and ring fingers of both hands. The swelling around the middle finger joints is spindle-shaped. No redness. The end finger joints look normal. Fingers are straight: no angling at the knuckles and no bent finger or thumb deformities. No nodules, scars or muscle wasting. Nails normal: no pitting, ridging, onycholysis or nail-fold lesions. No bony lumps at the end or middle finger joints, no squaring at the base of the thumb, no tophi, no sausage-shaped fingers.
  • Hands, inspection (palms): no wasting of the thenar or hypothenar eminences, no palmar erythema, no scars.
  • Elbows: no nodules, plaques or tophi. No swelling, warmth or tenderness.
  • Palpation: temperature of the wrists slightly warmer than the forearms. With the wrists slightly flexed, both are tender along the joint line, with soft, boggy, spongy swelling over the back of the wrist. Both ulnar styloids are tender. The 2nd and 3rd MCP joints of both hands and the 2nd, 3rd and 4th PIP joints of both hands are tender, with soft, spongy swelling. The DIP joints are not tender or swollen. Squeezing across the knuckles is painful in both hands.
  • Movement: she cannot press her palms flat together with the wrists bent back (prayer position), and the backs of her hands do not meet fully (reverse prayer). Wrist extension and flexion are reduced to about 50° each way and painful at the end of range. Making a fist: incomplete, fingertips 1 cm short of the palm in both hands. Finger joints otherwise move through range; no deformities to correct.
  • Special tests: Tinel's and Phalen's tests are negative on both sides. Sensation is normal in the median, ulnar and radial distributions.
  • Strength and function: thumb opposition is intact. Grip is weak on both sides because of pain. Key grip is painful but present. She does up a button slowly and writes slowly but legibly.
  • Feet: squeezing across the MTP joints is tender on both sides. No visible swelling, no MTP crowding or deformity, no tophi, no sausage toes, no psoriasis, no nail changes.
  • Other joints and entheses: shoulders, knees and ankles have no swelling or tenderness. Achilles tendons and plantar fascia insertions are not tender. Schober's test is normal (if done).
  • Cardiovascular, respiratory and abdomen: dual heart sounds, no murmur, no pericardial rub. Chest clear, no fine crackles. Spleen not palpable. No lymphadenopathy.

check.x: Professionalism
Hand hygiene, introduces self as a medical student, confirms her identity (name and date of birth) and gains consent for the history and examination.
Asks about pain before touching. Seats her with both hands resting on a pillow, exposes the arms above the elbows, asks her to remove rings and watch, and watches her face while examining gently.
check.d: Credit if she is asked about pain before touching and at least 2 of: pillow, exposure above the elbows, removal of rings/watch, watching her face.

check.x: Acknowledges her worry about her aunt's hands and her work, uses plain language, and describes the findings to the examiner as they go.
History
Characterises the joint symptoms:

kids.x: Joints: knuckles and middle finger joints of both hands and both wrists, symmetrical, end finger joints spared; balls of both feet sore in the morning.
Onset and course: started 3 months ago in the right knuckles, spread to both hands and wrists, slowly worse, with swelling (wedding ring now too tight).
Asks how long morning stiffness lasts (about 90 minutes) and finds it eases with use and is worse after rest: an inflammatory pattern.
Function and handedness: right-handed hairdresser struggling with scissors and blow-drying, cut back to 3 days; jars, buttons and writing are hard.

check.x: Asks about constitutional symptoms: marked fatigue; no fever, sweats or weight loss.

Screens for other causes and extra-articular features (SLE features, recent viral illness or contacts, sicca, respiratory symptoms, carpal tunnel symptoms): all negative; her son has had only childcare colds.
check.d: Credit if 2 of these domains are covered.

check.x: Screens for psoriatic arthritis and spondyloarthritis: psoriasis in herself and her family (father has psoriasis), nail changes, back pain or stiffness, red painful eyes, bowel symptoms.
check.d: Credit if 3 or more are asked, including psoriasis.

check.x: Takes the past history, medicines and allergies: no liver or kidney disease, hepatitis or TB; ibuprofen 400 mg two to three times a day from the chemist and the combined pill; allergy to Bactrim, and clarifies the reaction (widespread itchy rash).
check.d: The allergy and its reaction must be obtained for the mark.

check.x: Asks about contraception and pregnancy plans: on the combined pill, not pregnant, hoping to try for another baby in the next year or so.
Family history: aunt with deforming rheumatoid arthritis, father with psoriasis, mother with hypothyroidism.
Social history: hairdresser; lives with her husband and 4-year-old son; ex-smoker (about 10 a day from 18, stopped 5 years ago); a glass or two of wine on Saturday nights.
check.d: Credit if occupation and smoking are covered.

check.x: Explores ideas, concerns and expectations: she wonders whether work caused it, fears her fingers will bend like her aunt's and that she will not be able to work, and wants a diagnosis and effective treatment.
Examination
General inspection: comfort, habitus, Cushingoid features, aids or oxygen, malar rash, psoriasis and inflammatory eye disease. Asks for the vital signs (all normal, afebrile).
check.d: Credit if at least 3 general features are inspected and the vital signs are mentioned.

check.x: Inspects the backs and palms of both hands and describes:

kids.x: Symmetrical swelling of both wrists, the 2nd and 3rd MCPs and the 2nd to 4th PIPs (fusiform at the PIPs), with the DIPs spared.
No rheumatoid deformities: no ulnar deviation, swan neck, boutonnière or Z-thumb, and no nodules.
kids.d: Credit if at least 3 are named as absent.

kids.x: No features of other arthropathies: no Heberden's or Bouchard's nodes or squared thumb base, no tophi, no nail pitting, onycholysis or ridging, no dactylitis or plaques.
kids.d: Credit if at least 3 are named as absent.

kids.x: No redness, scars, or thenar, hypothenar or interosseous wasting; palms normal.

check.x: Inspects and palpates the elbows for rheumatoid nodules, psoriatic plaques, tophi, effusion and synovitis (none).
Palpates systematically and identifies active synovitis:

kids.x: Wrists in slight flexion: slightly warm, joint line tenderness and boggy swelling of both wrists, and tenderness of both ulnar styloids.
MCPs with both thumbs, and PIPs and DIPs bimanually: boggy, tender synovitis of the 2nd and 3rd MCPs and 2nd to 4th PIPs of both hands; DIPs normal.
kids.d: The candidate must call the soft, spongy swelling synovitis (not bony swelling) for the mark.

kids.x: Performs the MCP squeeze test: painful in both hands.

check.x: Assesses movement, special tests and function: prayer and reverse prayer signs (cannot complete), incomplete fist, Phalen's and Tinel's tests (negative), thumb opposition, grip and key grip (weak from pain), and a practical task such as a button or writing.
check.d: Credit if the prayer sign, Phalen's or Tinel's test, grip and one functional task are done.

check.x: Examines or states they would examine the feet (tender MTP squeeze on both sides; no tophi, dactylitis or psoriasis), and states they would complete the assessment with the eyes, heart (rub), lungs, spleen, spine (Schober's) and entheses.
check.d: Mentioning the feet earns the mark (source marking).

check.x: Interpretation
Checks the X-ray details: name and date of birth match Ms Little, date (10 days ago), right hand and wrist, PA and oblique views; notes only one hand was imaged.
Reads the X-ray systematically and identifies the features of early rheumatoid arthritis:
check.d: Source marking: credit 3 of the 4 features for the mark.

kids.x: Soft tissue swelling around the MCP and PIP joints and the wrist.
Periarticular osteopenia, best seen at the 4th PIP joint.
Loss of joint space at the MCP and PIP joints, with the DIPs preserved.
Marginal erosions at the 2nd and 3rd metacarpal heads and the 4th PIP joint.

check.x: Interprets the bloods:

kids.x: CRP 24 and ESR 38: active systemic inflammation.
RF 64 and anti-CCP 180 both positive (anti-CCP strongly): seropositive rheumatoid arthritis, which predicts erosive, more severe disease; a negative ANA argues against SLE.
Hb 112 with a normal MCV and platelets 432: likely anaemia of chronic disease with reactive thrombocytosis. Normal LFT and kidney function are the baseline for methotrexate.

check.x: States the diagnosis: early seropositive, erosive rheumatoid arthritis, supported by 3 months of symmetrical small-joint synovitis with DIP sparing, prolonged morning stiffness, raised CRP and ESR, positive RF and anti-CCP, and erosions on X-ray.
Gives at least 3 differentials, each with a reason for or against: psoriatic arthritis, SLE arthritis, viral polyarthritis (parvovirus B19), osteoarthritis.
check.d: Credit 3 or more, each with a reason.

check.x: Names rheumatoid arthritis and SLE as the conditions that classically spare the DIP joints, and contrasts osteoarthritis and psoriatic arthritis, which involve them.
check.d: RA and SLE must both be named for the mark (source answer).

check.x: Management

Explains in plain words that this is rheumatoid arthritis, not caused by her work. Early treatment can switch off the inflammation and protect her joints, so bent fingers like her aunt's are not inevitable.
check.d: May be credited from the answer to Ms Little's question about her aunt.

check.x: Starts methotrexate once weekly on a named day (never daily), building up over weeks, with folic acid on another day; no trimethoprim/Bactrim; limit alcohol.
check.d: Critical minimum: once weekly (never daily) and folic acid. Bactrim/trimethoprim avoidance and alcohol limit are credit-worthy extras. May be credited from the ISBAR Recommendation.

check.x: Arranges the pre-treatment checks: hepatitis B and C serology (HIV if at risk), a baseline chest X-ray and a pregnancy test.
check.d: Credit if hepatitis B serology and one other check are named. May be credited from the ISBAR Recommendation. A vaccination review before immunosuppression (influenza, pneumococcal, COVID-19, zoster, measles and varicella immunity) is a credit-worthy extra.

check.x: Addresses pregnancy: methotrexate can harm a pregnancy, so she needs effective contraception while taking it (continue the pill). When she wants to try for a baby she plans it with the rheumatologist, who stops methotrexate at least 3 months before she tries to conceive (ARA), continues folic acid, and switches to a pregnancy-compatible treatment such as hydroxychloroquine or low-dose prednisolone.
check.d: Critical minimum: states methotrexate can harm a pregnancy so she needs effective contraception while taking it, AND that a pregnancy is planned with the rheumatologist, who stops methotrexate months before she tries to conceive. The 3-month interval, folic acid and switch drug are credit-worthy extras. May be credited from the answer to Ms Little's pregnancy question or the ISBAR Recommendation.

check.x: Bridging: a short tapering corticosteroid course (oral prednisolone, or IM or intra-articular methylprednisolone) with paracetamol, and treat-to-target review with the rheumatologist.
check.d: Credit if a short bridging corticosteroid and rheumatology treat-to-target review are stated. Credit-worthy extras: a short-term NSAID if there is no contraindication; measuring disease activity (e.g. DAS28); referral to a hand therapist/OT; escalation through combination csDMARDs and then a PBS-subsidised bDMARD or tsDMARD; avoiding sulfasalazine because of her sulfonamide (Bactrim) allergy; a physiotherapist; Arthritis Australia patient education.

check.x: Safety netting

Gives specific red flags in plain words: see her GP the same day for fever, sore throat or mouth ulcers, unusual bruising or bleeding, a new cough or breathlessness, or yellow skin or eyes. Go to ED for a single hot, swollen joint with fever.
check.d: Credit if 3 or more are named in plain words.

check.x: Arranges follow-up: rheumatology clinic review in 4 to 6 weeks, a letter to her GP, and FBC, LFT and UEC every 2 to 4 weeks for the first 3 months or after a dose increase, then every 1 to 3 months.
check.d: Credit clinic review and regular blood monitoring; the exact interval is not required.

part2.lead: Here are the blood results her GP organised 10 days ago, and the report of the X-ray of her right hand and wrist taken the same day.
part2.patient:
During the third question, as the candidate explains the plan, Ms Little asks each of these once:

  • "So is it rheumatoid arthritis? Are my fingers going to end up bent like my aunt's?"
  • "We were hoping to have another baby next year. Can I still take this medicine?"

If the candidate uses jargon ("DMARD", "synovitis", "erosions"), ask "What does that mean?" once. She agrees to start methotrexate once the candidate explains that early treatment protects her joints and that a pregnancy can be planned safely with the rheumatologist.

handover.label: Blood results (GP, 10 days ago)
handover.result: Collected at her GP practice on 13/10/2026, before the rheumatology referral. No hepatitis serology has been done.
handover.model:
Read: CRP 24 and ESR 38 are raised. Rheumatoid factor is 64 (positive) and anti-CCP is 180 (strongly positive). ANA is negative. Hb 112 is mildly low with a normal MCV of 84. Platelets 432 are raised. White cells are normal. Electrolytes, creatinine and liver function are normal, with an eGFR above 90.

For Ms Little:

  • The raised inflammatory markers confirm active systemic inflammation.
  • Positive RF with a strongly positive anti-CCP fits seropositive RA. Anti-CCP is highly specific for RA and predicts erosive, more severe disease.
  • A negative ANA argues strongly against SLE.
  • The mild normocytic anaemia and reactive thrombocytosis are most likely anaemia of chronic disease. Iron studies are reasonable because she has taken ibuprofen for 2 months.

What it changes: she scores highly on the ACR/EULAR classification criteria and needs a DMARD started now. Normal liver and kidney function mean methotrexate can be used, and these results are its monitoring baseline. Hepatitis B and C serology, a pregnancy test and a chest X-ray are still needed before she starts.

labs.title: Urea, electrolytes, creatinine and liver function

handover.label: X-ray of the right hand and wrist
handover.result:
Patient: Sarah Little. DOB 29/01/1991.

Examination: X-ray of the right hand and wrist, PA and oblique views. Date of examination: 13/10/2026.

Clinical details: 35-year-old woman with 3 months of painful, stiff, swollen hands and wrists. ?Inflammatory arthritis.

Comparison: none available.

Findings:

  • Soft tissues: fusiform soft tissue swelling around the 2nd to 4th PIP joints and the 2nd and 3rd MCP joints, and soft tissue swelling over the wrist. No soft tissue calcification.
  • Bone density: periarticular osteopenia at the MCP and PIP joints, best seen at the 4th PIP joint. No generalised osteopenia.
  • Joint spaces: uniform loss of joint space at the 2nd and 3rd MCP joints and the 2nd to 4th PIP joints. The DIP joints are preserved.
  • Bone margins: small marginal erosions at the 2nd and 3rd metacarpal heads and at the 4th PIP joint. No osteophytes or subchondral sclerosis. No punched-out erosions with overhanging edges. No periostitis, pencil-in-cup change or tuft resorption.
  • Alignment: normal. No subluxation or deviation of the digits.
  • Other: no chondrocalcinosis. No fracture.

Conclusion: inflammatory, erosive arthropathy of the MCP and PIP joints, with periarticular osteopenia and DIP sparing. Clinical correlation is recommended.
handover.model:
Details: name and DOB match Ms Little. The film is 10 days old and shows the right hand and wrist only, PA and oblique views, with no comparison.

Read: soft tissue swelling around the MCPs, PIPs and wrist. Periarticular osteopenia, best seen at the 4th PIP. Uniform loss of joint space at the MCPs and PIPs, with the DIPs preserved. Marginal erosions at the 2nd and 3rd metacarpal heads and the 4th PIP. Alignment is normal.

For Ms Little: these are the radiological features of rheumatoid arthritis, and the erosions show it is already erosive at 3 months. The X-ray argues against the main alternatives:

  • osteoarthritis: no osteophytes, sclerosis or DIP disease
  • gout: no punched-out erosions with overhanging edges
  • psoriatic arthritis: no periostitis, pencil-in-cup or DIP erosions
  • CPPD: no chondrocalcinosis.

There are no deformities yet, which matches her examination.

What it changes: early erosions are a poor prognostic sign and support starting a DMARD now, with intensive treat-to-target care. Request X-rays of both hands and both feet (she has tender MTPs) as a baseline to judge progression.

ask: The rheumatology consultant has come into the clinic room. Please give an ISBAR handover of Ms Little, including your interpretation of these results.
What is your most likely diagnosis, and what else would you consider? Justify your answer.
Outline your management of Ms Little now, here in the rheumatology clinic, including what you would tell her before she leaves and the follow-up you would arrange.
Which conditions classically spare the DIP joints of the hand?
expect:
• Identify: self, medical student in clinic. Sarah Little, 35, hairdresser, GP referral.
  • Situation: 3 months of symmetrical pain, swelling and 90 minutes of morning stiffness in the hands and wrists; likely early RA.
  • Background: aunt with RA, father with psoriasis. Takes ibuprofen and the combined pill. Bactrim allergy (rash). Planning a pregnancy in about a year.
  • Assessment: synovitis of both wrists, 2nd and 3rd MCPs and 2nd to 4th PIPs, positive MCP squeeze, DIPs spared, no deformities; tender MTPs. CRP 24, ESR 38; RF and anti-CCP positive; ANA negative; mild normocytic anaemia; LFT and UEC normal. X-ray (name and DOB match): soft tissue swelling, periarticular osteopenia, joint space loss, marginal erosions; DIPs spared.
  • Recommendation: start weekly methotrexate after hepatitis serology, a chest X-ray and a pregnancy test; bridging steroid; contraception and pregnancy planning; X-rays of both hands and feet.

Most likely: early seropositive, erosive rheumatoid arthritis. Supporting features: symmetrical synovitis of the wrists, MCPs and PIPs with DIP sparing; tender MTPs; 90 minutes of morning stiffness; raised CRP and ESR; positive RF and strongly positive anti-CCP; marginal erosions and periarticular osteopenia on X-ray.

  • Psoriatic arthritis: her father has psoriasis. Against: no psoriasis, nail changes or dactylitis; DIPs spared; anti-CCP positive.
  • SLE arthritis: a young woman with DIP-sparing small-joint arthritis. Against: no rash, ulcers, alopecia or Raynaud's; ANA negative; erosive.
  • Viral polyarthritis (parvovirus B19): she has a child in childcare. Against: lasting 3 months, no rash in contacts, erosions.
  • Osteoarthritis: manual work. Against: age 35, inflammatory stiffness, no Heberden's or Bouchard's nodes or osteophytes.

1. Explain: rheumatoid arthritis; early treatment protects the joints, so deformity is not inevitable.
  2. Methotrexate once weekly on a named day, never daily (e.g. 10–15 mg, increased over weeks), folic acid on another day; no trimethoprim or Bactrim; limit alcohol. First: hepatitis B and C serology, chest X-ray, pregnancy test.
  3. Pregnancy: effective contraception (continue the pill); a planned pregnancy with the rheumatologist, stopping methotrexate ≥3 months before trying.
  4. Bridging: short tapering prednisolone or IM/intra-articular steroid; treat-to-target review.
  5. Safety net: same-day GP for fever, sore throat, mouth ulcers, bruising, cough or breathlessness, jaundice; ED for a hot swollen joint with fever.
  6. Follow-up: clinic 4–6 weeks, regular FBC/LFT/UEC, GP letter.

• Rheumatoid arthritis and SLE (Jaccoud's arthropathy) classically spare the DIP joints. Both affect the MCPs, PIPs and wrists.
  • By contrast, the DIPs are involved in osteoarthritis (Heberden's nodes) and psoriatic arthritis (often with nail pitting or onycholysis, and dactylitis). Gout can also affect a DIP joint.
  • So DIP involvement in a patient with polyarthritis points away from RA.

ddx.for: Three months of symmetrical synovitis of the wrists, MCPs and PIPs with DIP sparing, tender MTPs, 90 minutes of morning stiffness, raised CRP and ESR, positive RF and anti-CCP, and marginal erosions with periarticular osteopenia on X-ray.
Her father has psoriasis and she has an erosive polyarthritis of the hand.
ddx.against: No psoriasis, nail pitting, onycholysis or dactylitis, the DIPs are spared, there is no periostitis or pencil-in-cup change, and anti-CCP is strongly positive.

ddx.for: A young woman with a symmetrical, DIP-sparing small-joint arthritis and fatigue.
ddx.against: No rash, photosensitivity, mouth ulcers, alopecia or Raynaud's, ANA is negative, and the X-ray shows erosions, which SLE arthritis does not cause.

ddx.for: A symmetrical small-joint polyarthritis in a mother whose son attends childcare.
ddx.against: It has lasted 3 months rather than a few weeks, there is no rash in her or her contacts, and she has erosions and a strongly positive anti-CCP.

ddx.for: Hand pain in a hairdresser who uses her hands all day.
ddx.against: She is 35, with prolonged inflammatory morning stiffness, soft synovial rather than bony swelling, spared DIPs, no Heberden's or Bouchard's nodes and no osteophytes on X-ray.

guide:
In Part 1 the examiner gives findings from the Exam findings only when the candidate says what they are examining. Give the clinic nurse's vital signs when asked. Read the palpation findings as descriptions (soft, spongy, tender swelling): item 19 is earned only when the candidate names this synovitis and separates it from bony swelling. Allow about 3 to 4 minutes of history and 6 to 7 minutes of examination, which is the core of the station. Items 12–14 may be credited if covered briefly, e.g. a single family-history question that draws out the aunt's RA. Prompt at 4 minutes if the candidate has not started examining. Credit item 21 if the candidate mentions examining the feet (source marking). The pregnancy plans and the Bactrim reaction come out only when asked.

In Part 2, read the lead, hand over both results together, then ask the four questions in order. Ms Little puts her two questions during the third question. Item 25 may be credited from the ISBAR or the diagnosis answer. Item 28 is earned from the fourth question, but credit it if the candidate has already stated that RA and SLE spare the DIPs. Items 30 to 37 are earned mainly from the third question. Items 31 and 32 may be credited from the ISBAR Recommendation. Item 30 may be credited from the answer to Ms Little's question about her aunt. Item 11 may be credited if the candidate raises contraception or pregnancy plans with her in Part 2.

A high-performing candidate asks about morning stiffness, function and the screens for other arthritides, and asks about pregnancy plans. They prepare properly (pain, pillow, exposure, jewellery) and examine systematically: general inspection, look, feel and move, special tests and function, elbows and feet. They name the symmetrical synovitis with DIP sparing and the absence of deformities. In Part 2 they check the film's details and read it systematically. They diagnose early seropositive erosive RA and start weekly methotrexate after pre-treatment screening, linked to contraception and a planned pregnancy. They give specific safety netting and follow-up.

A borderline candidate inspects without palpating each joint group, or calls the swelling bony. They miss the feet, read the X-ray as osteoarthritis, or omit the date and identity check. They may prescribe methotrexate without stating that it is weekly, or without addressing contraception and pregnancy plans, or give vague safety netting.
explain:
Diagnosis: early seropositive, erosive rheumatoid arthritis

Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is a chronic, symmetrical, inflammatory polyarthritis of the synovium. It typically affects the MCP and PIP joints, the wrists and the MTP joints, and spares the DIP joints. The joint pain is inflammatory: worse after rest, with morning stiffness of more than 30 to 60 minutes, and easing with use. Fatigue is common. Ms Little has 3 months of symmetrical synovitis of the wrists, MCPs and PIPs, tender MTPs, 90 minutes of morning stiffness and fatigue. Her aunt's RA adds to her risk, and her past smoking is a recognised risk factor for seropositive RA.

On the 2010 ACR/EULAR classification criteria (a score of 6 or more out of 10 classifies RA) she scores 10:

  • more than 10 joints involved, including small joints: 5
  • high-positive anti-CCP: 3
  • raised CRP and ESR: 1
  • symptoms for 6 weeks or more: 1.

Erosions after only 3 months, a strongly positive anti-CCP and many involved joints are poor prognostic features. Untreated synovitis erodes cartilage and bone, and over time causes the fixed deformities (ulnar deviation, swan neck, boutonnière, Z-thumb) that her aunt has. Treatment started in the first months of disease gives the best chance of preventing them.

The rheumatological hand examination

  • Prepare: introduce yourself, gain consent, clean your hands. Expose above the elbows (the feet and precordium may be needed). Seat the patient with the hands on a pillow, and ask about pain first.
  • General inspection: distress, habitus, malar rash, psoriasis, inflammatory eye disease, Cushingoid features, aids and oxygen. Mention the vital signs.
  • Look at the hands, backs and palms: swelling and its distribution (are the DIPs spared?), erythema, thenar and hypothenar wasting, nail changes and scars. Look for the pattern of each arthropathy:
    • RA: swan neck, boutonnière, Z-thumb, ulnar deviation at the MCPs, nodules.
    • SLE: reversible deformities (Jaccoud's arthropathy).
    • Osteoarthritis: Heberden's and Bouchard's nodes, squared thumb base.
    • Gout: tophi.
    • Psoriatic arthritis: dactylitis, nail pitting, onycholysis, ridging, plaques.
  • Elbows: psoriasis, tophi and rheumatoid nodules; palpate for effusion and synovitis.
  • Feel (to show active inflammation):
    • With the wrist slightly flexed, feel for joint line tenderness, effusion, bogginess and ulnar styloid tenderness.
    • Palpate the MCPs with both thumbs, and the PIPs and DIPs bimanually.
    • Do the MCP squeeze test.
    • Synovitis is soft, warm and boggy; bony swelling is hard.
  • Move and special tests: prayer and reverse prayer signs, making a fist, Phalen's and Tinel's tests (carpal tunnel syndrome is common in RA). Test opposition and grip, and function (key grip, a button, writing).
  • Beyond the hands: feet (tophi, MTP crowding or tenderness, dactylitis, psoriasis), eyes, the heart (pericardial rub), lungs (interstitial lung disease), spleen (Felty's syndrome), Schober's test and the entheses.

Which conditions spare the DIP joints?

RA and SLE classically spare the DIPs. Osteoarthritis (Heberden's nodes) and psoriatic arthritis (often with nail disease and dactylitis) involve them, and gout can affect any joint. Finding DIP disease in someone with polyarthritis should make you reconsider RA.

Differentials

  • Psoriatic arthritis: can be symmetrical and erosive, and may precede the skin disease. A family history of psoriasis raises the possibility. Look for DIP disease, nail changes and dactylitis; radiologically, periostitis and pencil-in-cup change.
  • SLE: a non-erosive arthritis in young women, with rash, ulcers, alopecia, Raynaud's and a positive ANA. Deformities, if present, are reversible (Jaccoud's).
  • Viral polyarthritis: parvovirus B19 (common in parents of young children), Ross River and Barmah Forest viruses, and hepatitis B and C can mimic early RA. Parvovirus B19 arthritis usually settles within a few weeks. Ross River and Barmah Forest virus arthritis can persist for 3 to 6 months or longer, so ask about mosquito exposure and rash and consider serology when relevant. RF and anti-CCP are usually negative, and viral arthritis does not cause erosions.
  • Osteoarthritis: older patients, DIP and thumb-base disease, short stiffness, bony swelling.

Interpreting the results

  • Bloods: raised CRP and ESR show active inflammation. Anti-CCP is highly specific for RA. A strongly positive anti-CCP, like a high RF, predicts erosive disease. A negative ANA makes SLE very unlikely. Mild normocytic anaemia with thrombocytosis fits chronic inflammation; consider iron studies after 2 months of ibuprofen. Normal liver and kidney function are the baseline for methotrexate.
  • X-ray: always check the name, date of birth, date and views first. The early features of RA are:
    • soft tissue swelling
    • periarticular osteopenia
    • uniform loss of joint space
    • marginal erosions at the "bare areas", where synovium meets bone without cartilage cover, in the MCPs, PIPs and wrist (including the ulnar styloid).
    Later come subluxation and the zig-zag deformity. Contrast these with:
    • osteoarthritis: loss of joint space, osteophytes, subchondral sclerosis and cysts
    • gout: punched-out erosions with overhanging edges
    • psoriatic arthritis: DIP erosions, periostitis and pencil-in-cup change.
    Image both hands and both feet as a baseline; foot erosions often appear first.

Management (eTG Rheumatology: rheumatoid arthritis; RACGP early RA guideline)

  • Start a DMARD early. Methotrexate is first line. Give it once weekly on one named day, starting at a modest dose and increasing over the following weeks as tolerated. Give folic acid on a different day, e.g. 5 mg once weekly, to reduce side effects. Methotrexate may be combined with other conventional DMARDs (e.g. hydroxychloroquine). Sulfasalazine is contraindicated in Ms Little because of her sulfonamide (Bactrim) allergy.
  • Before starting: FBC, LFT and UEC (done here), hepatitis B and C serology (HIV if at risk), a baseline chest X-ray and a pregnancy test. Review vaccinations before immunosuppression, as set out in the Australian Immunisation Handbook (influenza, pneumococcal, COVID-19, and immunity to measles and varicella). If she is not immune to measles or varicella, give live vaccines at least 4 weeks before starting methotrexate and avoid pregnancy for 28 days afterwards. (The Australian Immunisation Handbook classes low-dose methotrexate as low-level immunosuppression; live vaccines during treatment are a specialist decision.) Consider recombinant zoster vaccine (Shingrix).
  • Pregnancy: methotrexate is harmful in pregnancy. Women taking it need effective contraception. A planned pregnancy is managed with the rheumatologist, who stops methotrexate at least 3 months before she tries to conceive (ARA), continues folic acid, and switches to a pregnancy-compatible treatment such as hydroxychloroquine or low-dose prednisolone. If disease is not controlled, the rheumatologist may use a pregnancy-compatible biologic (e.g. certolizumab). Ms Little's wish for another baby in about a year should be part of the plan from the first visit.
  • Bridging: a short, tapering course of corticosteroid (e.g. low-dose oral prednisolone, or IM or intra-articular methylprednisolone) controls symptoms while the DMARD takes effect over weeks to months. Avoid long-term use. Paracetamol, and an NSAID short term if there is no contraindication, help symptoms but do not change the course of the disease.
  • Treat to target: measure disease activity (e.g. DAS28) and aim for remission or low disease activity. If the target is not reached, escalate to combination conventional DMARDs. Leflunomide is best avoided in Ms Little because of her pregnancy plans: it is teratogenic and needs a cholestyramine washout before conception. Methotrexate plus hydroxychloroquine is the natural first combination. A rheumatologist can then prescribe a PBS-subsidised biological or targeted synthetic DMARD once the PBS criteria are met.
  • Team and long-term care: a hand therapist or occupational therapist (resting splints, joint protection, adapting her work), a physiotherapist, and the GP. RA raises cardiovascular risk, so manage blood pressure, lipids and smoking. Arthritis Australia provides patient education.

Safety netting and follow-up

  • Weekly dosing: methotrexate taken daily instead of weekly has caused deaths. State the dose and day on every script and in every explanation.
  • Interactions and alcohol: avoid trimethoprim and co-trimoxazole (Bactrim), which increase the risk of bone marrow suppression. Limit alcohol to no more than 1 to 2 standard drinks once or twice a week (ARA). Tell every doctor and pharmacist.
  • Same-day GP review for fever, sore throat, mouth ulcers, bruising or bleeding (cytopenia), a new cough or breathlessness (pneumonitis), or jaundice. ED for a single hot, swollen joint with fever.
  • Follow-up: rheumatology clinic in 4 to 6 weeks. FBC, LFT and UEC every 2 to 4 weeks for the first 3 months or after a dose increase, then every 1 to 3 months (ARA). A letter to the GP.
points: Examine the hands in order: prepare (consent, exposure above the elbows, pillow, ask about pain), general inspection, look at the backs and palms, elbows, feel each joint group, move with special tests and function, then the feet and the systemic features.

Early RA gives symmetrical, soft, boggy synovitis of the wrists, MCPs and PIPs with DIP sparing, a positive MCP squeeze, ulnar styloid tenderness and morning stiffness over 30 to 60 minutes, often before any deformity.
RA and SLE classically spare the DIP joints. DIP involvement points to osteoarthritis (Heberden's nodes) or psoriatic arthritis (nail pitting, onycholysis, dactylitis).

Early RA on X-ray: soft tissue swelling, periarticular osteopenia, uniform loss of joint space and marginal erosions. Check the name, date of birth, date and views first, and image both hands and feet as a baseline.

A strongly positive anti-CCP confirms RA and predicts erosive disease. Start a DMARD early: methotrexate once weekly, never daily, with folic acid on another day, after hepatitis B and C serology, a chest X-ray and a pregnancy test, and treat to target.
In a woman of child-bearing age, discuss contraception and pregnancy plans before starting methotrexate, and plan any pregnancy with the rheumatologist.
